summary: Specifies Proportional Integral controller Enhanced (PIE), an active queue management scheme that fights bufferbloat, where oversized buffers cause high delay. It drops packets probabilistically to keep queueing delay low. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: If a line at a shop gets too long, everybody waits forever. PIE sometimes turns people away early so the line stays short and moves fast.

subtitle: Active queue management that controls network latency to prevent bufferbloat

tldr.problem: Network buffers are often oversized to avoid packet loss, but oversized buffers cause packets to queue for a long time, resulting in high latency and latency variation that degrade interactive applications like VoIP and real-time video. Traditional queue management schemes like RED adjust dropping based on queue length, not the actual delay users experience.
tldr.mechanism: PIE (Proportional Integral Controller Enhanced) is an active queue management (AQM) scheme that measures queuing latency directly and uses a proportional-integral control loop to adjust the packet drop probability. When latency exceeds a target (e.g., 15 ms), PIE gradually increases the drop probability; when latency is low, it decreases it. This keeps average queue delay controlled without requiring careful per-packet timestamps.
tldr.outcome: Networks can achieve low, predictable latency while maintaining high link utilization. PIE has been adopted in cable modem standards (DOCSIS 3.1) and can be implemented in hardware and software with minimal overhead. It is experimental but has seen real-world deployment.

facts.label: Drop probability decay
facts.value: 0.98x per update (2% decay when congestion ends)

today: RFC 8033 is an Experimental protocol. PIE has been adopted in production systems, notably in the DOCSIS 3.1 cable modem specification mandated by CableLabs in 2013. It is also implemented in the Linux kernel (fq_pie queueing discipline) and is used in various network devices. The design addresses the bufferbloat problem identified in real networks and provides practical latency control for interactive applications.

sections.title: The Bufferbloat Problem
sections.content:
Bufferbloat is a phenomenon in which oversized network buffers cause excessive queuing latency. To achieve high throughput and avoid packet loss, network operators add large buffers to routers and switches. However, TCP continuously increases its sending rate until packets drop. By that point, the buffer is full, so all packets experience a long delay before transmission.

This causes real problems for interactive applications:

  • VoIP (voice over IP): delays above 150 milliseconds make conversations feel unnatural
  • Online gaming: high latency causes lag and poor responsiveness
  • Real-time video: high latency variation (jitter) causes video stuttering
  • Financial transactions: traders suffer losses if their orders are delayed

Traditional Active Queue Management (AQM) schemes like RED (Random Early Detection) drop packets based on queue length, not latency. When a queue reaches a threshold, they drop packets to signal congestion. But queue length is not the same as delay: a long queue on a slow link means long wait times, but the same queue on a fast link might clear quickly. PIE measures actual latency instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet used to have small buffers, but now they're huge—which helps move lots of data but makes everything slow because packets wait in line forever. PIE measures how long packets actually wait and tries to keep that short.

sections.title: Design Goals and Control Theory
sections.content:
PIE aims to achieve four goals:

1. Control Latency, Not Queue Length: PIE measures queuing delay directly (either via timestamps or by estimating queue length divided by dequeue rate). It uses a target latency (typically 15 milliseconds) and strives to keep the average delay near that target, regardless of how long the queue is.

2. High Link Utilization: Dropping packets too early starves the link; dropping too late causes bloat. PIE balances these extremes by gradually increasing drop probability as latency rises, giving TCP time to back off before the queue overflows.

3. Simple Implementation: Unlike RED, which requires careful tuning of queue thresholds for different networks, PIE uses fixed parameters chosen via control theory. Network operators need only set the target latency; the algorithm auto-tunes itself.

4. System Stability: PIE uses a Proportional-Integral (PI) controller, a classical control-theory design. The proportional term responds to how far latency is from the target; the integral term responds to the trend (is latency rising or falling?). This combination eliminates steady-state error and ensures stability across different network conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: PIE uses a simple control idea: if packets wait too long, drop more of them to reduce the queue. If they're waiting less, drop fewer. The "proportional" part responds to the current wait time; the "integral" part responds to whether it's getting worse or better.

sections.title: The PIE Algorithm
sections.content:
PIE has three main components:

Latency Calculation: PIE measures or estimates the current queuing latency. The simplest method is Little's law: latency = queue_size / dequeue_rate. Alternatively, PIE can timestamp packets at enqueue and calculate actual delay at dequeue, or estimate dequeue rate by measuring how long it takes to drain a threshold number of bytes from the queue.

Drop Probability Calculation: PIE periodically updates (every 15 milliseconds by default) the drop probability using the PI formula:

p = alpha * (current_latency - target_latency) + beta * (current_latency - previous_latency)

The first term (alpha) is proportional to how far current latency is from the target; the second term (beta) is proportional to the rate of change. If latency is 20 ms and target is 15 ms, and it was 18 ms last update (trending up), both terms increase the drop probability. If latency drops to 10 ms, the drop probability decreases.

PIE auto-scales alpha and beta based on the current congestion level, so the same parameters work across different link speeds and traffic patterns. When congestion eases (latency stays low), the drop probability decays exponentially at 2% per update, converging to zero quickly.

Random Dropping: On packet arrival, PIE randomly drops the packet with probability equal to the current drop probability. If the queue is very short or latency is very low, PIE skips dropping to remain "work-conserving" (not idle the link unnecessarily). After dropping decisions are made, packets are enqueued.
sections.plainLanguage: Every 15 milliseconds, PIE checks: "How long are packets waiting? Is it trending worse?" If yes, it increases how often to drop packets. If latency gets low, it stops dropping.

sections.title: Optional Enhancements and Deployment
sections.content:
Burst Tolerance: PIE allows short bursts of traffic (e.g., 150 milliseconds of traffic exceeding the target latency) without dropping. This protects against legitimate temporary spikes and short flows. A burst allowance counter starts at 150 ms and decrements every update period; as long as it's positive, packets are enqueued. When congestion clears (drop probability returns to zero), the counter resets.

ECN Support: PIE can mark packets with the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) flag instead of dropping them, if the drop probability is below a threshold (10% by default). ECN-capable endpoints detect the marking and reduce their sending rate without waiting for a packet loss, improving efficiency.

Dequeue Rate Estimation: When accurate timestamps are unavailable, PIE can estimate the dequeue rate by measuring how long it takes to drain 16 KB of data from the queue, updating the estimate as the queue drains. This trades a small latency measurement delay for simplicity.

Deployment Considerations: PIE should sit on top of a fair queuing structure (per-flow or per-class queuing) to ensure fairness across users. It is most effective on bottleneck links where buffering occurs. Modern implementations include PIE in Linux (kernel fq_pie discipline) and DOCSIS 3.1 cable modems.
sections.plainLanguage: PIE has optional extras: allowing brief traffic bursts, marking packets instead of dropping them if endpoints support it, and estimating link speed when you don't have timestamps.

left.title: RED (Queue-Length Based)
left.desc: Drop when queue exceeds threshold. Problem: doesn't account for link speed, so full queue might mean very different delays.

right.title: PIE (Latency-Based)
right.desc: Drop when queuing latency exceeds target. Adapts to link speed and traffic patterns automatically.
